newsitem.title: UK: Options - Coffee rally finally sees nervous signs.
newsitem.headline: Options - Coffee rally finally sees nervous signs.

text.p: Coffee's spectacular rally is finally making some investors dizzy, causing options interest to turn to puts after at least two solid weeks of call buying.
"There's been put interest in September at the $2,000 strike and higher," a broker said. "There's been minimal call interest because people are worried prices will slip off."
Coffee futures surged this week on continued supply woes and jitters before Brazil's frost season begins.
In New York, July arabicas rose sharply for three consecutive days. On Thursday, July leapt to more than $3.00 per pound to score a contract high and a fresh 20-year high.
Strong New York prices triggered a buying spree in London, pushing July robustas up nearly 20 percent on Thursday to reach just over a 20-month high.
Though no Brazil frost has been seen yet, analysts predicted more gains. Some said roasters caught on the wrong side of prices were scrambling to buy coffee at higher prices.

Options traders also said coffee got a boost when a large trade house still holding a 1,000 short Septemeber call position set about two weeks ago jumped into the futures buying spree to keep its position hedged. Traders said the trade house bought heavily on Wednesday to keep hedged as prices soared.
They said the short call positions between about the $2,000 and $2,300 strikes were still open.
With coffee climbing each day deeper into uncharted ground, volatilities have swelled. The front-end of the volatility curve was inverted, with September higher than July.
At-the-money implied September volatility settled near 69 percent on Thursday, up from last week's 60 percent. July and December were each seen near 60 percent.

September was seen bearing the brunt of the Brazil concerns. If a frost surfaces there, the extent of damage would be known in September. September, already considered a lean period for coffee supplies, could also feel another squeeze if a Brazilian drought emerges like it did in 1994.

In 1994, coffee prices surged when a drought followed a frost in Brazil. There have not yet been frost signs in Brazil, but some analysts are still wary. Some analysts have also started predicting a dry period for Brazil.

Cocoa options remained in coffee's shadows this past week, but traders noted some interest emerging in cocoa on Friday morning. Though no options traded, a few quotes were seen as some investors turn more friendly towards cocoa.
CSCE cocoa closed strong on Thursday and some technical analysts said London's July looked poised to test resistance at 1,050 stg per tonne and eventually, move to 1,200.
Options traders said in-the-money September calls were quoted this morning at 1,050 and 1,100.

At-the-money implied July volatility was pegged at 23 percent, down from about 30 percent a week ago. September fell to 25 percent from between 28.5 and 29 percent last week. Volatility eased because cocoa has spent most of its week in a tight range amid low volume.
